meta.subject: english
meta.description: Vocabulary facts: context clues, word relationships, synonyms/antonyms, homophones, homographs, idioms, roots/prefixes/suffixes, academic vocabulary, figurative language

facts.statement: A prefix is a word part added to the beginning of a base word that changes its meaning
The prefix 'un-' means 'not' or 'opposite of': unhappy, unkind, unfair
The prefix 're-' means 'again' or 'back': rewrite, return, replay
The prefix 'pre-' means 'before': preview, prepay, preschool
The prefix 'dis-' means 'not' or 'opposite': disagree, disappear, dislike
The prefix 'mis-' means 'wrongly' or 'badly': mistake, misspell, misunderstand
The prefix 'anti-' means 'against': antibacterial, antisocial, antithesis
The prefix 'inter-' means 'between' or 'among': international, interact, interstate
The prefix 'sub-' means 'under' or 'below': submarine, subway, submerge, subtitle
The prefix 'super-' means 'above' or 'beyond': superhero, supernatural, supermarket
The prefix 'over-' means 'too much' or 'above': overflow, overreact, overlook, overcome
The prefix 'non-' means 'not': nonfiction, nonsense, nonstop, nonprofit

common_errors.wrong: adding a prefix changes the spelling of the base word
common_errors.correct: Generally, adding a prefix does not change the spelling of the base word: un + happy = unhappy, mis + spell = misspell (double s is correct).

common_errors.wrong: all words starting with 'un' have the prefix un-
common_errors.correct: Some words starting with 'un' are base words, not prefixed: 'uncle', 'under', 'union' do not have the prefix 'un-.'

common_errors.wrong: 'dis-' and 'un-' always mean exactly the same thing
common_errors.correct: While both can mean 'not,' they attach to different words and are not always interchangeable. We say 'unhappy' not 'dishappy,' and 'disagree' not 'unagree.'

facts.statement: A suffix is a word part added to the end of a base word that changes its meaning or part of speech
The suffix '-ful' means 'full of': hopeful, beautiful, grateful
The suffix '-less' means 'without': hopeless, careless, fearless
The suffix '-tion' or '-sion' turns verbs into nouns: create/creation, decide/decision
The suffix '-ness' turns adjectives into nouns: happy/happiness, kind/kindness, dark/darkness
The suffix '-ly' usually turns adjectives into adverbs: quick/quickly, slow/slowly, happy/happily
The suffixes '-er' and '-est' are used for comparison: tall/taller/tallest, fast/faster/fastest
The suffix '-able' or '-ible' means 'capable of' or 'can be done': washable, readable, flexible, visible
The suffix '-ment' turns verbs into nouns meaning 'the act or result of': enjoy/enjoyment, govern/government, amaze/amazement
The suffix '-ous' or '-ious' means 'full of' or 'having': famous, dangerous, curious, mysterious

common_errors.wrong: -ful always means the same as the word 'full'
common_errors.correct: While '-ful' means 'full of,' the suffix is spelled with one 'l,' not two: hopeful, not hopefull.

common_errors.wrong: you always add -er or -est to compare adjectives
common_errors.correct: For longer adjectives (3+ syllables), use 'more' and 'most' instead: more beautiful, most interesting. Some adjectives are irregular: good/better/best.

common_errors.wrong: adding -ly always makes a word an adverb
common_errors.correct: Some -ly words are adjectives: friendly, lovely, lonely. Context determines the part of speech.

common_errors.wrong: -able and -ible follow the same spelling rule
common_errors.correct: Generally, '-able' is used with complete base words (washable, readable) and '-ible' with Latin roots (visible, flexible). There is no simple rule; many must be memorized.

facts.statement: About 60% of English words have Greek or Latin roots
The root 'bio' means 'life': biology, biography, biome
The root 'geo' means 'earth': geography, geology, geometry
The root 'graph' or 'gram' means 'write' or 'record': autograph, photograph, telegram
The root 'phon' or 'phone' means 'sound': telephone, phonics, microphone
The root 'scope' means 'to look at' or 'to see': telescope, microscope, periscope
The root 'auto' means 'self': autobiography, automatic, automobile
The root 'chron' means 'time': chronological, chronic, chronicle
The Latin root 'aud' means 'hear': audience, auditorium, audio, audible
The Latin root 'dict' means 'say' or 'speak': dictionary, dictate, predict, verdict
The Latin root 'port' means 'carry': transport, portable, import, export, report
The Latin root 'struct' means 'build': structure, construct, instruct, destroy (de + struct)

common_errors.wrong: knowing the root always tells you the exact meaning of a word
common_errors.correct: Roots give clues about meaning but words can evolve. Knowing roots helps with educated guesses, not exact definitions.

common_errors.wrong: all English words come from Latin
common_errors.correct: English has roots from many languages including Latin, Greek, Old English (Germanic), French, Norse, and others.

common_errors.wrong: Greek and Latin roots are only found in science words
common_errors.correct: Greek and Latin roots appear across all subjects and everyday language: 'telephone' (phone=sound), 'transport' (port=carry), 'biography' (bio=life).

facts.statement: Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings and spellings
'There' indicates a place, 'their' shows possession, and 'they're' is a contraction of 'they are'
'Your' shows possession, and 'you're' is a contraction of 'you are'
'To' is a preposition or infinitive marker, 'too' means 'also' or 'excessively,' and 'two' is the number 2
'Affect' is usually a verb meaning 'to influence'; 'effect' is usually a noun meaning 'a result'
'Than' is used for comparisons; 'then' refers to time or sequence
'Accept' means 'to receive'; 'except' means 'excluding' or 'other than'
'Principal' means 'main' or 'head of school'; 'principle' means 'a fundamental rule or belief'
'Its' shows possession (the dog wagged its tail); 'it's' is a contraction of 'it is' or 'it has'
'Weather' refers to climate conditions; 'whether' introduces a choice or alternative
'Hear' means to listen; 'here' means this place. A memory tip: 'hear' contains the word 'ear'

common_errors.wrong: their, there, and they're are interchangeable
common_errors.correct: Each has a distinct use: 'their' (possessive), 'there' (place/existence), 'they're' (they are). Example: They're going to their house over there.

common_errors.wrong: affect and effect mean the same thing
common_errors.correct: Usually, 'affect' is a verb (The rain affected the game) and 'effect' is a noun (The rain had no effect on attendance).

common_errors.wrong: it's okay to write 'could of' instead of 'could have'
common_errors.correct: 'Could of' is always wrong. The correct phrase is 'could have' (contracted as 'could've'), which sounds like 'could of' when spoken.

common_errors.wrong: 'its' needs an apostrophe to show possession
common_errors.correct: 'Its' (no apostrophe) is the possessive form. 'It's' (with apostrophe) is a contraction of 'it is.' This is the opposite of the usual apostrophe rule.

facts.statement: Context clues are hints found in the surrounding text that help readers figure out the meaning of unknown words
A definition clue directly states the meaning of a word in the same sentence: 'Nocturnal, meaning active at night, animals hunt in the dark'
A synonym clue uses a word with a similar meaning nearby: 'The jubilant, or joyful, crowd cheered'
An antonym clue uses a word with the opposite meaning: 'Unlike her timid sister, she was bold and confident'
An example clue provides examples that illustrate the unknown word: 'Citrus fruits, such as oranges, lemons, and grapefruits, are rich in vitamin C'
An inference clue requires the reader to use logic and background knowledge along with text clues to determine word meaning
Signal words like 'such as,' 'for example,' 'in other words,' 'meaning,' and 'or' often introduce context clues
Punctuation marks like commas, dashes, and parentheses can set off context clues within a sentence
Using context clues is a strategy readers apply before looking up a word in the dictionary

common_errors.wrong: context clues always give the exact dictionary definition
common_errors.correct: Context clues provide approximate meaning to help with comprehension. For the precise definition, a dictionary is needed.

common_errors.wrong: the context clue is always in the same sentence as the unknown word
common_errors.correct: Context clues can appear in the same sentence, the sentence before, or the sentence after the unknown word.

common_errors.wrong: if you can't find a context clue, the word has no meaning you can figure out
common_errors.correct: You can also use word parts (prefixes, roots, suffixes), background knowledge, or a dictionary when context clues are insufficient.

facts.statement: Synonyms are words with similar meanings: happy/joyful, big/large, fast/quick, sad/unhappy
Antonyms are words with opposite meanings: hot/cold, happy/sad, big/small, light/dark
Homographs are words that are spelled the same but have different meanings and sometimes different pronunciations: 'lead' (to guide) vs. 'lead' (a metal)
Homonyms are words that sound the same AND are spelled the same but have different meanings: 'bat' (an animal) vs. 'bat' (a baseball tool)
Denotation is the dictionary definition of a word; connotation is the feeling or association a word carries beyond its literal meaning
'Cheap' and 'affordable' have similar denotations (low cost) but different connotations: 'cheap' often sounds negative, 'affordable' sounds positive
An analogy shows a relationship between two pairs of words: hot is to cold as tall is to short (opposites relationship)
Multiple-meaning words have more than one definition: 'bank' can mean a financial institution or the side of a river
Synonyms are rarely exact; most have slight differences in shade of meaning: 'happy,' 'glad,' 'ecstatic,' and 'content' all mean pleased but differ in intensity

common_errors.wrong: synonyms mean exactly the same thing and can always replace each other
common_errors.correct: Synonyms have similar but rarely identical meanings. 'Walk' and 'stroll' are synonyms but 'stroll' implies a leisurely pace that 'walk' does not.

common_errors.wrong: homophone and homograph are the same thing
common_errors.correct: Homophones sound the same but are spelled differently (there/their). Homographs are spelled the same but may sound different (lead/lead).

common_errors.wrong: connotation is just another word for definition
common_errors.correct: Denotation is the literal definition. Connotation is the emotional association. 'Home' and 'house' denote a dwelling, but 'home' connotes warmth and belonging.

common_errors.wrong: every word has exactly one antonym
common_errors.correct: Some words have multiple antonyms (light: dark, heavy), some have none (the), and some antonyms depend on context (light as 'not dark' vs. 'not heavy').

facts.statement: An idiom is a phrase whose meaning is different from the literal meaning of its individual words: 'break a leg' means 'good luck'
'Let the cat out of the bag' means to reveal a secret, not to actually release a cat
'Hit the nail on the head' means to be exactly right about something
'Piece of cake' means something is very easy to do
'Under the weather' means feeling sick or unwell
'Once in a blue moon' means very rarely or almost never
A proverb is a short, well-known saying that expresses a general truth or piece of advice: 'Practice makes perfect'
Idioms are specific to languages and cultures; they often do not translate directly into other languages
'Bite off more than you can chew' means to take on a task that is too big or difficult for you
'Cost an arm and a leg' means something is extremely expensive

common_errors.wrong: idioms should be understood literally
common_errors.correct: Idioms are figurative expressions. 'It's raining cats and dogs' means heavy rain, not animals falling from the sky.

common_errors.wrong: idioms and proverbs are the same thing
common_errors.correct: An idiom is a figurative expression (kick the bucket = die). A proverb is a wise saying that gives advice (the early bird catches the worm).

common_errors.wrong: idioms are grammatically incorrect
common_errors.correct: Idioms follow normal grammar rules; their special feature is that their meaning cannot be determined from the individual words.

facts.statement: Academic vocabulary includes words used frequently across school subjects, such as 'analyze,' 'compare,' 'evidence,' 'summarize,' and 'evaluate'

Tier 1 words are basic, everyday words most children know (dog, happy, run); Tier 2 words are high-utility academic words (analyze, compare, formulate); Tier 3 words are domain-specific (photosynthesis, legislature)
'Compare' means to examine similarities between things; 'contrast' means to examine differences between things
'Summarize' means to restate the main points briefly in your own words, leaving out minor details
'Infer' means to use clues and evidence to figure out something that is not directly stated
'Evidence' refers to facts, examples, quotes, or data that support a claim or answer
'Analyze' means to break something down into parts to understand how it works or what it means
'Evaluate' means to judge the quality, value, or importance of something based on criteria or evidence
'Cite' means to refer to a source or piece of evidence to support a point; 'text evidence' is information taken directly from a reading passage
'Synthesize' means to combine information from multiple sources to form a new understanding or conclusion

common_errors.wrong: summarize and retell are the same thing
common_errors.correct: A retell includes all events in order. A summary includes only the main points and key details, leaving out less important information.

common_errors.wrong: infer and guess are the same
common_errors.correct: A guess is random. An inference is based on evidence and reasoning — it is a logical conclusion supported by clues.

common_errors.wrong: compare means the same as contrast
common_errors.correct: Compare examines how things are alike. Contrast examines how things are different. 'Compare and contrast' means to examine both similarities and differences.

common_errors.wrong: academic vocabulary is only needed for tests
common_errors.correct: Academic vocabulary appears in textbooks, instructions, news articles, and professional communication. Understanding these words is essential for all reading comprehension.

facts.statement: Figurative language means words or phrases that go beyond their literal (dictionary) meaning to create a special effect or image
A simile compares two unlike things using 'like' or 'as': 'She runs like the wind' or 'He is as tall as a tree'
A metaphor compares two unlike things by saying one thing IS another: 'The classroom was a zoo' means it was chaotic
Personification gives human traits to nonhuman things: 'The flowers danced in the breeze'
Hyperbole is a huge exaggeration used for emphasis or humor: 'I'm so hungry I could eat a horse'
Onomatopoeia is a word that sounds like what it describes: crash, buzz, sizzle, meow, whoosh
Understanding the difference between literal and figurative meaning is essential: 'He has a heart of gold' does not mean his heart is made of gold
Alliteration repeats the same beginning sound in nearby words: 'Sally sells seashells by the seashore'

common_errors.wrong: similes and metaphors are the same thing
common_errors.correct: A simile uses 'like' or 'as' to compare (fast as a cheetah). A metaphor states the comparison directly without 'like' or 'as' (he IS a cheetah on the field).

common_errors.wrong: personification means a person is in the sentence
common_errors.correct: Personification gives human qualities to NONhuman things. 'The sun smiled down' gives a human action (smiling) to the sun.

common_errors.wrong: figurative language is wrong because it is not literally true
common_errors.correct: Figurative language is intentionally non-literal. It makes writing more vivid, creative, and expressive. It is a deliberate writing choice, not an error.
